intro: In the middle of the 1970s, skateboarding left the sidewalk and went looking for curves. Skaters in Southern California found them in empty backyard pools. New urethane wheels and smooth bearings let them grip the walls and climb toward the coping. In 1976 the first concrete skateparks opened, and by the end of the decade there were dozens of them.

Then the parks began to close, and skaters had to find new places to ride. They built wooden ramps in backyards and turned to the street. A no-hands jump from Florida, the ollie, moved from ramp walls to flat ground. Videos on tape and new magazines carried each new trick across the country.

In this unit you will learn the people, places and dates of the pool and park years and the 1980s. You will name the parts of a pool and a ramp. You will use real physics to explain why a skater feels heavy in a curve, how height becomes speed, and how an ollie pops a board into the air.
bigQuestion: How did empty pools, new wheels and one no-hands trick change where people skate and what they can do?

timeline.t: Frank Nasworthy's Cadillac Wheels bring urethane wheels to skateboards
Larry Stevenson's kicktail patent is granted
The Zephyr team skates the Del Mar Nationals
Carlsbad Skatepark and Skateboard City open; a drought empties pools
Alan 'Ollie' Gelfand pops no-hands airs on ramp walls in Florida
Thrasher magazine begins in San Francisco
Rodney Mullen does the ollie on flat ground
Powell Peralta releases The Bones Brigade Video Show
The Search for Animal Chin is released

words.d: the curved part of a ramp or pool where the flat floor bends up into the wall
the rounded lip along the top edge of a pool or ramp
short for vertical; the part of a wall that goes straight up and down
a tough, rubbery plastic used for skateboard wheels since the early 1970s
a place built for skateboarding, with ramps, bowls and curves
a turn or trick where the skater's chest and toes face the wall or obstacle
stored energy that something has because of its height
the energy something has because it is moving
a jump where the skater pops the tail and the board rises with the feet, with no hands
the turning effect of a force, found by force times the distance from the pivot
an ollie in which the front foot flicks off the toe-side edge so the board flips along its long side
skating on things found in a town, such as curbs, ledges and banks

test.q: What left many Southern California pools empty in 1976 and 1977?
test.why: The drought of 1976 and 1977 meant less water, so some pools sat empty.

choices: the curved part at the bottom of a wall
the part of a wall that goes straight up and down
the flat floor of a pool
the metal pipe on a ramp
test.why: Vert is short for vertical, the straight-up part above the transition.

test.q: Who sold urethane wheels through Cadillac Wheels in the early 1970s?
test.why: Frank Nasworthy's Cadillac Wheels brought urethane wheels to skateboarding.

test.q: Which skatepark opened in Port Orange, Florida, in 1976?
test.why: Skateboard City opened in Port Orange in 1976, the same year as Carlsbad in California.

test.q: What closed many skateparks in the early 1980s?
test.why: Rising insurance costs and injury lawsuits made many parks too costly to run.

test.q: With no friction, about how fast is a skater moving after rolling down from a height of 1 meter?
test.why: 2 times 9.8 times 1 is 19.6, and its square root is about 4.4 meters per second.

test.q: As a skater rolls down a pool wall, what happens to their energy?
choices: kinetic energy turns into potential energy
potential energy turns into kinetic energy
test.why: Height energy becomes motion energy on the way down.

test.q: Why does a skater feel heavier at the bottom of a curved transition?
choices: Gravity is stronger at the bottom
The floor must hold them up and also turn them around the curve
test.why: The floor's push supports their weight and supplies the centripetal push, so it adds up to more.

test.q: In a frontside air, where does the skater's chest face?
test.why: Frontside means the chest and toes face the wall or obstacle.

test.q: Who did the ollie on flat ground in the early 1980s?
test.why: Gelfand's ollie was on ramps. Rodney Mullen brought it to flat ground.

test.q: In an ollie, what is the pivot the board turns around?
test.why: When the tail is snapped down, the board turns around its back wheels and the nose rises.

test.q: In an ollie, what lets the front foot drag the board upward?
choices: friction from the rough grip tape
test.why: Grip tape is rough, so friction lets the shoe pull the board up as it slides.

test.q: Which skater rode for the Bones Brigade?
test.why: Steve Caballero was a member of Powell Peralta's Bones Brigade.

test.q: In what year did TransWorld SKATEboarding begin?
test.why: TransWorld SKATEboarding began in 1983, two years after Thrasher.

test.q: What is the safest first object to ollie onto when learning street skating?
choices: a low painted curb away from cars
test.why: Start small and low, away from traffic, and add height only when landing feels easy.

write.prompt: Explain how the ollie changed skateboarding. Name Alan Gelfand and Rodney Mullen and when each one did the trick. Then explain the steps of an ollie and the physics behind them: the lever, Newton's third law, friction from grip tape, and hang time for a 0.30-meter ollie.
tips: Start with where the ollie began, on ramp walls in the late 1970s.
Say what changed when the ollie moved to flat ground in the early 1980s.
Put the ollie's steps in order: crouch, snap, slide, jump, level, land.
Show the hang-time arithmetic step by step with g = 9.8 m/s².
Finish with one safe first step for a new learner.
